newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish new finance minister vows quicker reforms.
newsitem.headline: Polish new finance minister vows quicker reforms.

text.p: Poland's new Finance Minister Marek Belka vowed on Wednesday to speed up the country's transition to a free market, saying that sustainable growth and a radical inflation cut were impossible without faster reforms.
Belka said he would use his position of the deputy prime minister in charge of the economy to press ahead with the lagging privatisation and much-delayed crucial reform of the social security system.

"I will get engaged in the issue of privatisation. I will use the forum of the government's economic council to monitor its progress and speed up things," Belka said at his first news conference since he took his post early in February.
He said he would specifically make sure that the privatisation of several banks and telecommunications monopoly TPSA goes as planned.

The government officials earlier said that two large banks, Bank Handlowy SA and Powszechny Bank Kredytowy SA, will be privatised in 1997. Privatisation of TPSA is due to begin this year, with a first public share issue expected in 1998.
Belka became the finance minister earlier this month after his predecessor Grzegorz Kolodko resigned, saying he wanted to avoid being involved in campaign to this year's parliamentary elections.
Belka vowed after his nomination to pursue Kolodko's policy of financial discipline and macroeconomic stability.

Belka confirmed on Wednesday that fight against inflation was his priority but said that no spectacular success in this area was possible unless the current sound macroeconomic policies are accompanied with structural reforms.

Those include quicker privatisation, cutting subsidies to ailing state-owned firms and an overhaul of the pension system, which, if left unreformed, may undermine public finances in the longer term, he said.
"Our inflation is so persistent because Poland's economic transformation has not been completed. It is difficult to fight inflation with only monetary and budget policies," he said.
In the last four years the government had repeatedly missed its original inflation targets.
Last year inflation fell to 18.5 percent from 21.6 percent in 1995 but fell short of the original target of 17 percent, which initially had been targetted for 1995..
Belka described the current monetary policy, carried out by the central bank in consultations with the finance ministry, as "moderately restrictive" and said it should not change.
